children: Many banks, including State Bank of India (SBI), Punjab National Bank and Union Bank of India, have issued a customer advisory ahead of the three-day nationwide bank strike proposed by the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) from September 28 to 30, 2026. The proposed strike comes after the UFBU's one-day nationwide strike on September 11 and is part of the union forum's wider programme, which also includes a continuous strike from October 26.

While the strike is expected to affect banking operations, questions also arise over what happens to employees' salaries during such industrial action. A bank employee explained that whenever a strike is called by bank unions, employees participating, or not, in the strike generally do not receive salary for those days.
"If this strike happens, I may not receive a total of four days’ salary, which would impact my monthly budget," said a Scheduled Bank employee, who requested anonymity.
What is the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU)?

The UFBU is an umbrella platform of bank employee and officer organisations that comes together to take up issues at the industry level. Rather than being a single trade union, it brings together multiple unions representing employees and officers across the banking sector.
When the UFBU calls an industry-wide strike, the participating unions generally act together, making it different from a strike called by an individual union at a particular bank.

"When it is an industry-level call, the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) is the umbrella organisation under which all the participating bank employee organisations come together. So, when UFBU gives a strike call, all the organisations generally participate. There is no question of one particular union opting out. Moreover, in such strikes, UFBU members do not receive salary for those days, as the principle of 'no work, no pay' applies," said Bikash Narayan Mishra, a former banker who writes on social and public policy issues.

The proposed September 28-30 action therefore needs to be viewed differently from a strike called only by one union or at an individual bank. The participation and impact can depend on the unions involved and whether branches and offices remain operational.

"Of course, if someone is not a member of any of these organisations, they have the right to decide whether or not to participate. If such an employee reports for work but finds that the office is closed because of the strike, their attendance can be marked accordingly, and they should not face a salary deduction for that day," said Mishra.

There can also be specific exemptions. For instance, if an employee is due to retire in that particular month, they may be exempted because a loss of pay could have an impact on their pension-related calculations.
UFBU strike vs bank-level strike: What is the difference?
The distinction between an industry-wide UFBU strike and a bank-level strike is important when determining who is likely to participate.

"Broadly, when UFBU gives an industry-level strike call, employees across the participating organisations take part. This is different from a bank-level strike. At the bank level, if the majority union gives a strike call, it does not necessarily mean that members of minority unions will participate. Similarly, if a minority union calls a strike, participation may be limited. So, those are essentially partial or bank-specific strikes, whereas a UFBU call is an industry-wide action," said Mishra.
